hints: Grimm's Law: an initial Latin p- regularly becomes English f-.
It swims; Pisces is the zodiac sign of two of them.
Four letters, starts with F.
fact: Latin piscis → English fish is the textbook Grimm's Law pair: PIE *p became Germanic *f. The same shift gives pater/father and ped-/foot.

hints: Two shifts in one word: Latin p- → English f-, and Latin t → English th.
He's your male parent; the word survives in 'paternal'.
Six letters, starts with F.
fact: pater → father shows the Grimm chain twice: *p→f and *t→th. Spanish padre only got one change away from Latin.

hints: Latin p- → English f- (Grimm's Law).
You stand on two of them; see 'pedestrian' and 'podiatrist'.
Four letters, starts with F.
fact: Latin pes, pedis → English foot. The d in the stem was lost in the Germanic branch: *ped- → *fōts.

hints: Latin t- → English th- (Grimm's Law).
It's between two and four; trio, triple, triangle.
Five letters, starts with T.
fact: tres → three: PIE *t became English th but stayed t in Latin (tres), German shows the third outcome: drei.

hints: Latin t- → English th-.
The old singular 'you', now mostly heard in wedding vows and Shakespeare.
Five letters, starts with T.
fact: Latin tu → English thou (both from PIE *tuH). The German cousin is 'du' — the three pronouns match sound for sound.

hints: The ct cluster of Latin often hides a simple English gh that went silent.
The opposite of day; nocturnal, equinox.
Five letters, starts with N.
fact: noct- → night: the gh was once pronounced [ç] in English, cousin to German Nacht and Spanish noche.

hints: Latin d- → English t-, Latin t → th: a two-step chain.
You brush them; dentist, trident, dandelion ('lion's tooth').
Five letters, starts with T.
fact: dent- → tooth is Grimm's Law doubled: PIE *d→t and *t→th. German Zahn took a third road via the High German shift.

hints: Latin c- (a k sound) often becomes English h-.
Trumpets and rhinos have them; cornucopia is the 'horn of plenty'.
Four letters, starts with H.
fact: cornu → horn: PIE *k stayed k in Latin (cornu) but became h in Germanic. Spanish cuerno and German Horn complete the set.

hints: Latin c- → English h-.
Ten tens; the word hides in 'century' and 'percent'.
Seven letters, starts with H.
fact: centum → hundred: the same k→h shift as cornu/horn. Linguists literally name language branches 'centum' vs 'satem' after this word.

hints: Latin c- → English h-.
Man's best friend; canine, kennel.
Five letters, starts with H.
fact: canis → hound: 'dog' is the upstart Norse word that displaced the older hound, which lives on in 'greyhound' and German Hund.

hints: This one is near-identical: only the vowel shape changed.
Not old; novel, novice, innovate.
Three letters, starts with N.
fact: novus → new: sometimes the cipher is just vowel drift. Greek néos gives us 'neon' — literally the 'new one' gas.

hints: Look past the vowels; the consonants n-m-n map one-to-one.
What your parents call you; nominal, noun, nominate.
Four letters, starts with N.
fact: nomen → name: PIE *h₁nómn̥. The Sanskrit twin is nā́man — some words barely changed in 5,000 years.

hints: Ignore the diminutive ending -ella; the st- root is the key.
Twinkle twinkle; stellar, constellation.
Four letters, starts with S.
fact: stella (a diminutive 'little star') and English star both descend from PIE *h₂stḗr, which also gives Greek astḗr → 'astronomy' and 'disaster' (bad star).

hints: Latin t between vowels → English th.
She's your female parent; maternal, matrix, matter.
Six letters, starts with M.
fact: māter → mother: the kinship suffix -ter is visible in mother, father, brother and daughter — a complete PIE family album.

hints: Latin f- at the start of a family word often points to a Germanic b-.
Male sibling; fraternal, fraternity.
Seven letters, starts with B.
fact: frater → brother: PIE *bʰ became Latin f and Germanic b. Spanish hermano lost the f entirely on the way down from Latin.

hints: Only one consonant moved — into a double letter.
Roman soldiers were partly paid in it; salary, salad, saline.
Four letters, starts with S.
fact: sāl → salt: German Salz shows the High German t→z shift, while Greek háls hides in 'halogen' — the salt-forming elements.

hints: Latin pl- simplifies to English f- plus a single l.
The opposite of empty; plenty, plenary, replenish.
Four letters, starts with F.
fact: plenus → full: Spanish lleno doubled the l instead. The same *pl- → f shift appears in primus → first.

hints: Latin pr- becomes English f- (yes, really).
Before all the others; primary, prime, premier.
Five letters, starts with F.
fact: primus → first: the flashiest Grimm pair after piscis/fish. PIE *p always yields English f when the word is native.

hints: Latin t- → English th-; the ending -are just means 'to'.
What follows lightning; the Norse god Thor has the same root.
Seven letters, starts with T.
fact: tonāre → thunder: Latin t → English th, and the -d- was added in Germanic. Spanish tronar kept everything but the accent.

hints: Latin t- → English th-; both words describe passing.
'From one side to the other'; transport, transit, transparent.
Seven letters, starts with T.
fact: trans → through: both from PIE *terh₂- 'to cross'. The English gh was once pronounced, like the ch in German 'durch'.

hints: Latin t- → English th-.
Not thick; the word hides in 'tenuous' and 'attenuate'.
Four letters, starts with T.
fact: tenuis → thin: a crisp demonstration that Latin t and English th are the same sound wearing different centuries.

hints: Latin v- (pronounced w-) maps to English w-.
Made from grapes; vine, vinegar, vineyard.
Four letters, starts with W.
fact: vīnum → wine: Latin v was actually a w-sound, so the two words sounded nearly identical 2,000 years ago.

hints: This one is nearly a freebie — say the Latin aloud.
Snake's delivery mechanism; the word is a cousin of 'Venus' (charms, potions).
Five letters, starts with V.
fact: venēnum → venom: borrowed through French from Latin, so it kept its shape. The native Germanic cognate of the root is 'win(n)' — strife.

hints: Latin v- = w-, so think w- words.
Empty, lacking; 'vanity', 'evanescent', 'wane'.
Four letters, starts with V or W.
fact: vānus → vain/wane/want: one Latin root scattered into three English words depending on which branch carried it.

hints: Greek k- → English h- when the word is native Germanic.
It beats in your chest; cardiac, cardiology.
Five letters, starts with H.
fact: kardía → heart: PIE *ḱ became k in Greek, h in English, s in Russian (serdtse). Three branches, three sounds, one word.

hints: The Greek lost a consonant English kept silent.
Goddess of the dark; nyctalopia is night-blindness.
Five letters, starts with N.
fact: nýks → night: Greek dropped the -t- of PIE *nókʷts that survives (silently) in English night and audibly in German Nacht.

hints: Greek d- → English t-: the same double-step as Latin dens.
Mastodon = 'breast tooth'; orthodontist straightens them.
Five letters, starts with T.
fact: odoús → tooth: Greek, Latin and Germanic each applied their own shift to PIE *h₃dónts — 'the biter' (from the verb 'to eat').

hints: Greek k- → English h-.
Cynics were literally 'dog-like' philosophers; cytology is not this root.
Five letters, starts with H.
fact: kýōn → hound: 'cynic' comes from the Cynics being teased as dogs. Sanskrit śvā shows the satem shift of the same root.

hints: Swap the ending and smooth the vowel.
Neon, neologism, Neolithic — all brand new.
Three letters, starts with N.
fact: néos → new: the neon sign is etymologically tautological — the 'new gas'.

hints: Greek keeps the s- that Latin and Germanic also kept — this one is about the tail.
Astronomy, asteroid, disaster.
Four letters, starts with S.
fact: ástron → star: a 'disaster' is literally a bad star — astrology written into English luck.

hints: The consonants n-m map directly; the vowels drifted.
Onomatopoeia = 'name-making'; synonym = 'with-name'.
Four letters, starts with N.
fact: ónoma → name: English 'name', Latin nomen, Greek onoma, Sanskrit nāman — a four-branch match on a single root.

hints: Greek h- can hide an s- that English kept at the end.
Halogen, halite (rock salt).
Four letters, starts with S.
fact: háls → salt: Greek lost the initial s (as Latin nix lost it from snow) — vowels and edges erode, consonant cores survive.

hints: English th → German d is the single most productive pair in the family.
Male sibling; Brüderlichkeit is 'brotherliness'.
Seven letters, starts with B.
fact: Bruder → brother: PIE *bʰréh₂tēr → German Bruder, English brother, Latin frater, Sanskrit bhrātar. One word, five passports.

hints: tt in German often stands where English puts th.
Rain, sun, and clouds; the German word covers both 'weather' and 'wetter'.
Seven letters, starts with W.
fact: Wetter → weather: the same th/d pair as Bruder. If you know one rule you own ~1,800 German words.

hints: German z is pronounced 'ts' — a shifted English t.
The base of the decimal system; see also 'zehnmal' = ten times.
Three letters, starts with T.
fact: zehn → ten: the High German consonant shift turned Germanic *t into z/ss — the same law that gives Wasser/water and Zeit/time.

hints: German ss often corresponds to English t after a vowel.
H₂O in every German beer garden.
Five letters, starts with W.
fact: Wasser → water: both from PIE *wódr̥, whose other branch gives Greek hýdōr — hydrogen is 'water-generator'.

hints: English th → German d, word-initially.
What you say when the Kellner brings the Bier; 'danke schön'.
Five letters, starts with T.
fact: danken → thank: English kept the th, German the d — thank/thank-you and danke are the same word said two ways.

hints: German ch [x] is what English gh used to sound like.
Gute Nacht! says itself.
Five letters, starts with N.
fact: Nacht → night: English gh went silent after the Great Vowel Shift, which is why 'night' no longer sounds like German 'Nacht'.

hints: English k after a vowel → German ch.
Buchstaben — 'book-sticks' — is the German word for letters.
Four letters, starts with B.
fact: Buch → book: the High German shift k→ch. Buche (beech tree) is related — early Germanic writing was carved on beech boards.

hints: German z [ts] ↔ English t.
Zeitgeist, literally 'the spirit of the ___'.
Four letters, starts with T.
fact: Zeit → time/tide: Old English tīd meant both. 'Yuletide' preserves the older sense; time took the abstract one.

hints: English gh ↔ German ch; the -en is just the verb ending.
What you do at a joke; Gelächter is laughter.
Five letters, starts with L.
fact: lachen → laugh: another gh/ch pair like Nacht/night. English spelling is a museum of sounds we lost.

hints: English d at the start of a word → German t.
What you do with Bier; ein Getränk is a beverage.
Five letters, starts with D.
fact: trinken → drink: the d/t swap of Tag/day and Tanz/dance — products of the High German consonant shift, ~500 AD.

hints: Latin p- inside a Spanish word points to English f-.
El padre de la familia; paternal.
Six letters, starts with F.
fact: padre → father: Spanish is Latin worn smooth, so every Spanish p-word is a hint that English may have an f-cousin.

hints: The n- root is unchanged; watch the vowels dance.
¡Año nuevo! Brand ___ year.
Three letters, starts with N.
fact: nuevo → new: from Latin novus. French neuf, Italian nuovo — the Romance family disagrees only about the ending.

hints: Spanish d- → English t-; and Latin ct became Spanish ch on the way.
El diente — you have 32; dentist is the borrowed double.
Five letters, starts with T.
fact: diente → tooth: from Latin dentem. Noctem → noche shows the same ct→ch Spanish signature.

hints: Spanish ch often collapses a Latin ct; the English cousin hides a silent gh.
Buenas noches.
Five letters, starts with N.
fact: noche → night: three languages, one PIE word — Latin noctem, Spanish noche, German Nacht, English night.

hints: Germanic w- corresponds to Romance gu-.
An oddly Germanic-looking word in Spanish — it was borrowed early; 'guerrilla' is its little version.
Three letters, starts with W.
fact: guerra → war: Spanish borrowed this from Germanic *werra. The same w/gu pairing gives ward/guardia and William/Guillermo.

hints: In Germanic, fj- often simplifies to plain f-.
What birds are covered in; Swedish fjäder is also an archaic 'spring' (it bounces).
Seven letters, starts with F.
fact: fjäder → feather: German Feder, Dutch veer, English feather — the whole Germanic branch agrees on this one.

hints: Dutch v- often maps to English f-.
Vaderlijk = fatherly. Yes, Darth Vader is literally 'Dark Father' in Dutch.
Six letters, starts with F.
fact: vader → father: Dutch sits between English and German — vader/father/Vater is the whole Grimm spectrum in one row.

hints: Sanskrit m- stays m- everywhere; it's the -t- that turned to th in English.
Mātā in Hindi today; the -r is an old case ending.
Six letters, starts with M.
fact: mātar- → mother: the Sanskrit, Latin (māter), Greek (mḗtēr) and English words match consonant for consonant — PIE's most durable word.

hints: Only the final vowel moved.
Nava- is the root behind Spanish nuevo and Greek neon — same family, different branch.
Three letters, starts with N.
fact: nava → new: from 'new' to 'novel' to 'neon' — the root is one of the most-traveled words in the world's languages.

hints: French wore the Latin word down to three sounds.
Bonne nuit!
Five letters, starts with N.
fact: nuit → night: French deleted more of noctem than any sibling — from two syllables to one, from ct to a mere glide.

hints: Italian p- → English f- (Grimm again).
You order it grilled at the trattoria; piscatorial is its Latin uncle.
Four letters, starts with F.
fact: pesce → fish: Italian just softened Latin piscis (sc → sh-sound); English ran it through the Grimm grinder.

hints: Slavic v- corresponds to English w- (both from PIE *w).
Add a diminutive and you get a famous clear spirit.
Five letters, starts with W.
fact: voda → water: vodka is 'little water' — the diminutive of the same PIE *wódr̥ that gives English water and Greek hydro-.

hints: Latin -ul- diminutives often shrink; the o-k consonants map to a vowel + gh in English.
Binocular, oculist — the seeing organ.
Three letters, starts with E.
fact: oculus → eye: English 'eye' comes from the Germanic branch of the same root (augō → Auge, öga), a different formation of 'the seer'.

hints: The same PIE root *wed- that gives English 'water' took a d-suffix in Latin.
Undulate, abundant ('overflowing'), inundate.
Five letters, starts with W.
fact: unda → water: not a letter-for-letter match — a root-level cognate. The d of unda and the t of water are cousins.
